# The Country of Night

There is a species of darkness that almost nobody alive has seen. Not the darkness of a bedroom with heavy curtains, nor the brown gloom behind closed eyelids, nor even the theatrical dark of a cinema, which is really a kind of dimness with pictures in it. I mean the original darkness — the kind that pressed against every human being who ever lived before the nineteenth century, and against most who lived long after. It is worth pausing on how recently we lost it. Your great-grandparents probably knew it. You almost certainly do not.

To meet it, you have to go looking, and even then it hides. You drive past the last town, past the last farm, down a dirt road onto some high plain far from any highway, and when you finally switch off your headlights you discover that a car's dome light, a phone screen, even the red standby eye of a camera will ruin everything. So you stand in the black and switch everything off, and at first there is nothing at all: no floor, no horizon, no hand when you wave it inches from your own face. Panic arrives quickly, and it is an old panic, older than language — the body's suspicion that darkness means danger, that the eyes have died.

But then, minute by minute, the eyes do what millions of years of night taught them to do. Shapes surface. The plain returns, gray on black. And the sky begins to do something extraordinary: it stops being a ceiling and becomes a depth. Stars separate from stars. Faint clouds of light resolve into structures. Under sufficiently dark skies the Milky Way is not a smear but a river — wide, textured, bright enough, some observers insist, to cast a faint shadow, as Venus sometimes does on white sand. The ground seems to dissolve beneath you. Many people report a mild vertigo on first seeing this, as though the earth had become optional. What they are feeling, presumably, is the sudden absence of a boundary their brains assumed was load-bearing.

In January 1994, an earthquake knocked out power across Los Angeles, and in the blacked-out hills residents looked up and saw a vast, luminous, silvery cloud arching over the city. Some called observatories. Some, unnerved, called emergency services, wondering whether the strange glow was connected to the quake. It was the Milky Way. Enough Angelenos had never seen their own galaxy that the sight of it registered as an anomaly — an omen, a malfunction, a threat.

What happened to Los Angeles in a single night has happened to our species over a century and a half. We did not simply illuminate the night. We deleted it, and along with it a whole wing of human experience that we barely remember possessing.

⁂

Before artificial light, night was not merely the absence of day. It was a jurisdiction with its own laws. Work stopped because it had to; travel ceased; communities contracted around fires and bolted doors. But contraction is not the same as death, and the premodern night was crowded with life. The historian Roger Ekirch, whose book *At Day's Close* reconstructs the hours of darkness from diaries, court depositions, sermons, ballads, and proverbs, portrays a world in which night was a distinct realm of activity — feared, yes, but also used. Crime moved at night; so did courtship, celebration, conspiracy, and worship. Rules bent. Masks went on. Night belonged to lovers and thieves and to anyone whose business thrived on not being seen.

It also belonged to the imagination, which in darkness is the only lamp available. With vision failing at the margins, the mind supplies its own images — a coat on a hook becomes a figure, a wind in the thatch becomes a voice. Every culture populated the dark with beings, and it is tempting to see this not as superstition alone but as accurate reporting: darkness really is inhabited, by the projections of the brain that watches it. Hypnagogic imagery, the hallucinations that bloom in the borderlands of sleep, were once a nightly public event rather than a curiosity of sleep clinics. Night was participatory. You did not observe it; you negotiated with it.

One of Ekirch's most striking findings concerns how our ancestors actually slept. Across centuries of documents, from medieval England to colonial America, he kept encountering a peculiar phrase: *first sleep*. People rose after it, or referred back to it, or lay waiting for it. Piecing the records together, he concluded that preindustrial humans typically slept in two segments. After dusk came the "first sleep," lasting several hours; then people woke naturally around midnight into a calm, drowsy, distinctly pleasant interval — contemporaries described it as unusually serene — and stayed awake for an hour or more before drifting into a "second sleep" that carried them to dawn. This was not insomnia. It was architecture. Laboratory work has since lent the idea support: when volunteers are given fourteen hours of darkness per night, their sleep reliably splits into two phases separated by quiet wakefulness, much as it apparently always did when the night was long. Consolidated eight-hour sleep, on this view, is not human nature but an artifact of the lightbulb.

And the midnight interval was not dead time. Records show people praying, reading by banked embers, talking softly with bedmates, visiting nearby kin, smoking, reflecting on the vivid dreams of the first sleep — which they tended to take seriously, as messages. Physicians recommended sex in this interval, arguing conception came easiest when both partners were rested and relaxed. Monasteries, meanwhile, had institutionalized the same rhythm for centuries: the office of Vigils existed precisely because the human body wakes in the middle of the night and asks for something to do. The dark hours contained a furnished room that we have since bricked over. Anthropologists working among the Tiv of Nigeria in the mid-twentieth century recorded the same idiom — first sleep, second sleep — still in daily use, suggesting the pattern runs deeper than any one culture's habits.

⁂

How did we lose it? Fuel by fuel. The oldest lamps were stone bowls holding animal fat; such lamps have been recovered from the depths of painted Paleolithic caves, where artists carried fire underground to work on walls no daylight could reach — the first galleries were lit galleries, and the first audiences sat in absolute black. Later came rushlights, tallow candles (cheap, smoky, foul-smelling), and beeswax (clean, costly, reserved for altars and the rich). For most of history, light was rationed like medicine. Peasants went to bed at dusk not because they were lazy but because staying awake cost money.

The first industrial escalation came from the sea. The head of the sperm whale holds a cavity of waxy oil that burns brighter and cleaner than almost anything else nature offers, and in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries entire economies organized themselves around harvesting it. Whaling fleets sailed for years to render leviathans into lamp fuel; drawing rooms in Boston and London glowed with rendered whale. It is a strange thing to realize: *Moby-Dick*, which looks like an epic of vengeance, is secretly an epic of illumination. Then coal gas, piped through city mains — London's Pall Mall was lit by gas in 1807, and soon the lamplighter with his pole became a fixed figure of the urban evening — and then petroleum, whose cheap kerosene all but finished the whale-oil trade by the 1860s, saving the sperm whale almost incidentally. Finally came Edison: a practical carbon-filament bulb in 1879, a generating station on Pearl Street in Manhattan in 1882, and light ceased to be a substance you purchased and became a utility you forgot. Within a single human lifetime, night shrank from a foreign country to a dim suburb of day.

Look at Earth from orbit tonight and you will see the result: a planet veined with light, a circuit board caught mid-thought. By one influential estimate, more than eighty percent of North Americans and a third of all humanity can no longer see the Milky Way from where they live. True darkness survives only in fragments — deserts, open ocean, the high latitudes — and even there it is eroded by gas flares and the floodlit decks of fishing fleets.

⁂

The costs are easier to measure than the losses. Sea turtle hatchlings, evolved to sprint toward the bright horizon of moonlit surf, are lured instead toward beachfront glow and crawl inland to die in parking lots; whole coastal towns now mandate amber, shielded fixtures to give the turtles back their moonlight. Migrating birds navigate by stars and skylight, and city glow pulls them off course into towers and glass; collisions with buildings kill birds in the hundreds of millions each year in the United States alone. Even the moth at the flame, emblem of fatal attraction, turns out to be a subtler tragedy: a study published in 2024 suggests insects aren't drawn to lights so much as destabilized by them. Many flying insects steer by keeping their backs to the brightest thing in view — normally the sky — and a lamp scrambles their sense of up, sending them into hopeless spirals. We did not seduce the night's creatures; we broke their instruments.

Our own instruments fare little better. Specialized cells in the human retina, tuned most sensitively to blue light around 480 nanometers, feed directly into the brain's master clock, suppressing melatonin and telling the body it is noon. Evening screens and bluish-white streetlamps push our bedtimes later and fragment our rest; shift work that forces wakefulness against the circadian tide is classified by international cancer researchers as probably carcinogenic, partly through precisely these mechanisms. Meanwhile the astronomers — the people with the strongest professional claim on the night — have been retreating uphill for a century, siting telescopes on ever more remote peaks, fighting losing battles against the glow of spreading suburbs.

⁂

Honesty, though, forbids pure elegy. The old night was not uniformly precious to those who lived in it. For the poor, the sick, the elderly, and above all for women, night historically meant danger sharpened: pain worse in the dark, help impossibly far, violence emboldened. Winter darkness meant hours awake in cold houses, hungry, waiting for a dawn that felt slow as geology. Reading by firelight ruined eyesight; literacy itself limped until cheap light let ordinary people read after work. The Romantics wrote gorgeous hymns to night by candlelight, warm and fed, which is one way of saying that darkness was romanticized chiefly by those who could afford lamps. Streetlight's relationship to crime turns out to be scientifically complicated — some studies find reductions, others mere displacement — but its effect on the *feeling* of safety is not complicated at all. Electric light emancipated as much as it erased. Any defense of darkness worth making must concede this and change the terms accordingly: the goal is not to fall back into the old night, which was compulsory and often cruel, but to choose darkness the way we choose wilderness — protected, accessible, voluntary. Nobody proposes abolishing farms to save the wild. The same logic applies here.

⁂

What, finally, is the case for the dark? Begin with something almost mechanical. Vision in low light depends on a pigment called rhodopsin, which the rod cells of the retina manufacture and bleach; full dark adaptation takes thirty to forty minutes, and a single flash of white light wipes it out instantly. This is a physical fact with a moral shape. Attention works the same way. Under constant illumination the pupil contracts; so does the mind. Darkness removes the external screen, and the mind, having nothing to watch, begins to project — dream, memory, image, idea. The night was humanity's first cinema and its first church, and both institutions still bear its fingerprints.

All the oldest stories, after all, are star stories. Constellations were the first archive: myth, season, and direction encoded in memorable figures pinned to a reliable ceiling. Egyptian priests timed the Nile's annual flood by tracking the dawn rising of Sirius and built a calendar on it; the pyramids align with stars. Polynesian navigators crossed thousands of miles of featureless Pacific by memorizing the rising and setting points of stars, reading swells and bird flight, holding an entire continent-sized chart in trained memory — navigation as a feat of the dark. Modern astronomy descends directly from this nightly necessity. Science has ancestors, and many of them worked the night shift.

The mystics said it more radically. St. John of the Cross, imprisoned in sixteenth-century Toledo, wrote of the "dark night of the soul" — darkness not as mere absence but as the paradoxical medium in which the deepest seeing occurs. A generation before him, the poet Novalis composed his *Hymns to the Night*, praising night as the opening onto the infinite, the condition under which the boundless announces itself to creatures otherwise distracted by surfaces. One need share none of the theology to notice how often the pattern recurs: withdraw the stimulus, and depth appears. The contemplative traditions converged on this independently — enclosure, silence, vigil — as if they had all discovered the same physics of the interior.

⁂

Which brings us, unexpectedly, to conservation. The International Dark-Sky Association, founded in 1988 by two astronomers, now certifies parks and reserves around the world where darkness is actively managed — shielded fixtures, spectral limits, lighting curfews — as a resource, the way water quality is managed. The first designated Dark Sky Park was Natural Bridges National Monument in Utah, in 2007; New Zealand protects the darkness over Aoraki Mackenzie by law. The engineering required is embarrassingly cheap: aim lights down, use warmer colors, switch off what serves no one. Much of the night sky could be returned to most of humanity for the price of better fixtures and slightly revised habits.

But fixture standards are the shallow layer of the argument. The deeper conservation is experiential, and it comes down to something almost embarrassingly simple: everyone should see the Milky Way at least once, ideally young. Not as spectacle — as address. Standing under it, you eventually understand that you are not looking *at* the galaxy the way you look at a painting. You are inside it. That pale river is the disk of our own home seen edge-on from within, and the sun you missed noticing set is one unremarkable star among a quarter trillion, adrift in one arm of the spiral. No lecture conveys this. Only the dark does, because only the dark is large enough.

We conquered the night so thoroughly that we forgot it was ours — half our inheritance, the other hemisphere of human life, the room where the imagination keeps its furniture. Darkness is not the enemy of light; it is light's context, the page under the ink. Meaning lives in the contrast, and we have been spending the contrast down like a fossil fuel.

So: go somewhere dark. Switch everything off. Wait half an hour — that is how long it takes, rhodopsin willing, to remember.

Para 1: Open with the strangeness that darkness—an experience universal to every generation until ours—is now nearly extinct. Most readers alive today have never known true darkness outside a cave or a cinema. Even countryside glows orange on the horizon.

Section: Night as a country. Before artificial light, night was half of existence with its own laws. Travel stopped; communities contracted; different rules applied (Ekirch: night was "a distinct sphere of activity"). Crime, spirits, ghosts—but also license, festivity, intimacy. Night as frontier between the living and other things. Every culture populated darkness with beings—because in darkness the mind generates its own light, hallucination at edges of vision; hypnagogic imagery. Night was participatory: you didn't observe it, you negotiated with it.

Segmented sleep: Ekirch's discovery—documents from diaries, letters, court records, medical books across centuries: people slept in two segments. "First sleep" after dusk; then waking of an hour or more around midnight—calm, drowsy, meditative interval; people prayed, read by ember-light, talked with bedfellows, visited neighbors, made love (physicians even recommended it then as most restful/conducive to conception), reflected on dreams which were taken seriously as messages. Then "second sleep" till dawn. References appear in Chaucer ("her firste sleep"), in prayer manuals designed for that interval. Anthropologists among the Tiv in Nigeria in the mid-20th century found the same pattern named in their language. The hypothesis: consolidated eight-hour sleep is an artifact of electric light; given darkness, mammals—humans included—default to biphasic rest. The midnight hour wasn't insomnia; it was a room in the house of night, furnished with its own activities. When light abolished the long dark, the room was bricked over. Some sleep researchers (Wehr's experiments: subjects given 14 hours of darkness developed segmented sleep) support it.

Conquest section: The technologies of light. Fire, then lamps burning animal fat—stone bowls at Lascaux; rushlights; tallow candles smoky and smelling; beeswax for churches and rich. For most of history a candle was a luxury item—labor measured against light. Then whale oil: the sperm whale's head full of spermaceti burned brighter and cleaner than anything; fleets sailed years hunting leviathans to light drawing rooms; cities ran on rendered whale. Moby-Dick is a book about light, though it seems about revenge. Then gas manufactured from coal piped through streets early 1800s—Pall Mall 1807—lamplighters with poles at dusk became figures of the city; then kerosene struck from rock oil in 1850s saved the whale almost incidentally; then Edison's carbon-filament bulb (1879) and the Pearl Street generating station (1882)—light became infrastructure, invisible as weather. Within a single lifetime, night went from another country to a dim suburb of day. Today satellites photograph Earth at night: a nervous system of glowing filaments; darkness survives only in patches—deserts, seas, Siberia, central Africa's less electrified regions—and even there, gas flares and fishing fleets' lights show.

Costs section: Ecology first. Sea turtle hatchlings evolved to sprint toward the bright horizon of moonlit surf; beachfront sodium lamps lure them inland, into pools and roads—communities now mandate amber low-spectrum fixtures. Migrating birds navigate by stars and magnetic fields; city glow draws them off course into towers; collisions kill hundreds of millions yearly in the U.S. alone (estimates). Insects: the moth-and-flame puzzle—2024 study suggests moths aren't "attracted" but confused: their dorsal light response assumes the brightest point is the sky/up; a lamp scrambles their sense of vertical, so they spiral. Whatever the mechanism, insect declines and nighttime pollination disrupted. Human bodies: melanopsin cells tuned to ~480nm blue suppress melatonin; evening screens and LED streetlight spectra push bedtimes later, fragment sleep; shift work classified as probable carcinogen partly via circadian disruption. Astronomers flee: observatories sited on remote peaks still fight encroaching glow; some cities dim.

Balance: Yet honesty forbids pure elegy. Pre-electric night was terror for many: women, the poor, travelers, the ill—night was when pain sharpened and help was far; winter nights meant cold hours awake in hunger. Streetlight was emancipation as much as loss; the ability to walk home safely, to read past dusk (reading by firelight damaged eyes; literacy spread with cheap light), to extend the working and social day—these were freedoms. The Romantics could aestheticize night because they had candles and hearths. Any defense of darkness must admit it was defended, historically, mostly by those who could afford lamps. The goal is not to re-enter the old night but to choose it—to preserve it the way we preserve wilderness: accessible, protected, voluntary.
